posts.text: Re: AI, people just don't seem much change in their lives. With most major tech innovation - rail, cell phones, computers, the internet, et al - it was obvious that ordinary life would differ in useful ways. With AI, it's not.
posts.summary: Skeptical that AI delivers tangible utility gains compared to past innovations
posts.quote: Re: AI, people just don't seem much change in their lives. With most major tech innovation - rail, cell phones, computers, the internet, et al - it was obvious that ordinary life would differ in useful ways. With AI, it's not.

posts.text: I listened to @TheStalwart and @tracyalloway interview Goldman's CIO Marco Argenti about AI. Argenti just didn't have any actual tangible explanations of how AI was useful. It was very abstract. He talked about how employees built travel apps in their spare time. But it's a bank!
posts.summary: Criticizes Goldman Sachs executive for lacking concrete explanations of AI usefulness
posts.quote: I listened to @TheStalwart and @tracyalloway interview Goldman's CIO Marco Argenti about AI. Argenti just didn't have any actual tangible explanations of how AI was useful. It was very abstract. He talked about how employees built travel apps in their spare time. But it's a bank!

posts.text: I know of use cases, things like summarizing meetings and phone calls, or doing first drafts of research, or helping with coding. These are real. But it's not the same thing as what the railroads did, or even cell phones. It just seems piddling.
posts.summary: Acknowledges narrow AI use cases but argues they lack transformative scope of past technologies

ai-technology.quote:
If Anthropic employees are actually developing nuclear weapons-style technology and also think they will become generationally wealthy off of taking risks the rest of humanity must bear, then they need to be jailed immediately.

Of course they are actually just bullshit artists.

Re: AI, people just don't seem much change in their lives. With most major tech innovation - rail, cell phones, computers, the internet, et al - it was obvious that ordinary life would differ in useful ways. With AI, it's not.

I listened to @TheStalwart and @tracyalloway interview Goldman's CIO Marco Argenti about AI. Argenti just didn't have any actual tangible explanations of how AI was useful. It was very abstract. He talked about how employees built travel apps in their spare time. But it's a bank!

I know of use cases, things like summarizing meetings and phone calls, or doing first drafts of research, or helping with coding. These are real. But it's not the same thing as what the railroads did, or even cell phones. It just seems piddling.
